title: Weighing by an electronic balance
objective: Zero (tare) a balance correctly before weighing
Read a digital balance to its stated readability
Weigh a sample by difference so any residue left behind is caught
Recognise an unstable/drifting reading and know its likely cause

theory.statement: Quantitative chemistry starts with an accurate mass. A modern electronic balance displays mass directly (unlike a null beam balance), but using it correctly still requires taring the container, waiting for the reading to settle, and reading no more digits than its stated readability justifies.
theory.derivationNote: Weighing 'by difference' — weighing the container plus solute, then weighing the container again after transferring the solute out — gives the mass actually transferred, and automatically detects any solid left clinging to the container. A single weighing of an empty container assumed to be exactly a round number can hide a real, uncorrected error.
keyEquations: Net mass = gross reading − tare (container) mass
Mass transferred (by difference) = mass before transfer − mass after transfer

apparatus.name: Weighing bottle / watch glass
apparatus.why: Container for the sample; never weigh a chemical directly on the pan

apparatus.name: Spatula
apparatus.why: Transfers solid without touching it by hand

apparatus.name: Sample (salt, coin, or similar)
apparatus.why: The object or substance to be weighed

procedure.text: Check the balance is level and switch it on; allow it to warm up if required.
Place the empty container on the pan and press tare/zero.
Add the sample with a spatula, close any draft shield, and wait for the reading to stop changing.
Record the stable reading to the balance's full readability.
Repeat the weighing to check repeatability.
Compare the two readings and comment on the balance's precision.

steps: Tare the balance with the empty container
Add the sample and wait for a stable reading

expectedResult.quantity: Net mass of the salt sample
expectedResult.statement: Correctly tared and read, the electronic balance gives a net mass of about 5.126 g, repeatable to well within its stated readability.

safety: Never weigh a chemical directly on the pan — use a container.
Do not weigh hot objects; convection currents give an unstable, drifting reading.
Clean any spillage on the pan immediately.
sourcesOfError: Forgetting to tare includes the container's mass in the result.
A draught or vibration prevents the reading from settling.
A hygroscopic solid gains mass steadily if left open to the air.

viva.question: Why must a chemical never be weighed directly on the pan?
viva.expectedConcept: It can corrode or contaminate the pan, and a corrosive or reactive chemical can damage the balance itself. A container also allows the mass to be tared away.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking a quick wipe afterwards is sufficient protection.

viva.question: What does 'weighing by difference' mean, and why is it more reliable?
viva.expectedConcept: Weighing the full container, transferring the sample out, then weighing the container again — the difference is the true mass transferred, automatically correcting for any solid left behind.
viva.answerLogic: Catches incomplete transfer that a single weighing would miss.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing a single careful weighing is equivalent.

viva.question: Two readings of the same sample differ by 0.02 g on a balance readable to 0.01 g. Is this balance faulty?
viva.expectedConcept: Not necessarily — some variation between 0.01 g readings is expected from air currents, static, or minor sample changes; 0.02 g is only two least counts. It becomes concerning only if it is persistent and much larger than the readability.
viva.answerLogic: Small scatter near the least count is normal, not a fault.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating any disagreement as an instrument fault.

preLab.question: Taring a balance means:
options: Setting the display to zero with a container already on the pan
preLab.feedback: Taring zeroes the display so subsequent readings show only the net mass of what is added.

duringLab.question: Weigh the sample at least twice to check repeatability.

postLab.question: State the net mass of the salt sample (g).

assumptions: No draughts or vibration during weighing
edgeCases: Weighing a hot or hygroscopic sample never truly settles
expectedBehaviour: Repeated weighings agree to within the balance's readability
